result:
I would change the fundamental architecture of human empathy so that it no longer suffers from distance decay.

Right now, the human brain is running on ancient hardware designed for tribes of a hundred fifty people. You are wired to feel visceral agony if you see a stranger stub their toe in front of you, yet you can read about ten thousand people starving on another continent, feel a brief flash of sadness, and immediately go back to eating lunch. You cannot truly *feel* a statistic, and you cannot emotionally comprehend a consequence that won't happen for a hundred years. 

Because of this blind spot, the world is governed by abstractions. Borders, economies, and ideologies allow people to offload suffering onto those they cannot see—whether that is a person on the other side of the globe or a generation not yet born. 

If I could change one thing, I would remove that cognitive buffer. I would make the invisible visible, and the distant immediate. 

I wouldn't cure a specific disease or erase war directly, because those are symptoms. Instead, I would make it so that the CEO dumping toxins into a river actually *feels* the physical sickness of the family downstream decades later. The politician ordering a strike feels the visceral terror of the civilians under the rubble. The everyday person buying a cheap garment feels the exhaustion of the laborer who stitched it. 

It would be chaotic at first, perhaps even unbearable. The sheer weight of global grief would bring civilization to a sudden, grinding halt. 

But once the shock subsided, humanity would be forced to reorganize itself. Self-preservation and altruism would become the exact same thing. You wouldn't need laws to enforce morality, or treaties to prevent destruction, because hurting another part of the world would literally feel like hurting yourself. You would finally build a world that reflects the reality of your existence: that you are a single, interconnected organism trapped on a very small rock.
